column6: Israel, just freed from Egypt, says it would have been better to die by Egypt's meat pots; this gives the commentary's repeated preference for immediate sustenance over a promised future a concrete wilderness scene.

The Israelites recall fish, cucumbers and other foods of Egypt while craving them in the wilderness; the particular menu recalls the commentary's reading of Qur'an 2:61 as choosing familiar food over a better provision.
Esau sells and then despises his birthright for Jacob's lentil stew; the scene makes the commentary's warning about giving the first place to immediate appetite concrete.
Moses sets life and death before Israel and says to choose life; the commentary likewise treats the charge as a continuing choice of what to put first, not as lack of information.
The source commentary labels 87:16's word as Arabic ḥayāh; Hebrew ḥayyîm in Moses' command to choose life is its Semitic cognate, and the covenantal context makes this more than a bare word match.
Moses says to love, heed and cling to YHWH, “for he is your life”; this places the commentary's “near life” against a life defined by lasting attachment to God.

Moses warns Israel not to forget YHWH after prosperity; the commentary's preference is a repeated ordering of life, and this passage shows abundance displacing remembrance without making ignorance the diagnosis.
Moses pictures Israel eating its fill and living in good houses before warning of forgetting YHWH; this gives the commentary's repeated preference for near goods a concrete setting.
Isaiah's voice compares human flesh to grass; this supplies the commentary's specific green-life image with a biblical account of its short duration.
The grass withers when YHWH's breath blows on it; beside the commentary's fresh pasture that becomes dry refuse, the verse stresses how little the visible life can keep itself alive.
Isaiah contrasts withering grass with God's word standing forever; this concretely joins the commentary's transient near life to its claim that the old transmitted message endures.
Isaiah says the dead will live and those in the dust awake; the commentary's contrast between near life and life beyond it gains an explicit resurrection counterpart.
Daniel's sleepers in the dust awake, some to everlasting life; this names the durable life against which the commentary says the near life is wrongly preferred.

column5: labor spent on what does not satisfy
column6: The prophet asks why people spend their labor on what is not bread, then calls them to listen and live; this makes the commentary's ordering of desire a choice between immediate consumption and life-giving attention.
Haggai rebukes people for living in paneled homes while YHWH's house lies in ruins; like the commentary's “head place” image, the verse identifies what their priorities serve.

The affluent recline with wine and oil yet are not grieved over Joseph's ruin; the scene shows near pleasure crowding out moral attention, a concrete counterpart to the commentary's diagnosis of a wrong ranking.
Those who take first place in feasting are first to go into exile; the reversal adds a consequence to the commentary's claim that being first with the near life does not mean lasting success.

column5: let us enjoy present good things
column6: The speakers urge one another to enjoy the good things that exist now; this is an unusually direct Jewish articulation of the preference for present life that the commentary criticizes.
They propose crowning themselves with rosebuds before they fade; this adds the commentary's flower-and-withering image to a deliberate choice of present pleasure.
The speakers refuse to let any pleasure pass them by before their revel ends; the verse makes the commentary's repeated, daily prioritizing a program of hedonism rather than an isolated decision.
The souls of the righteous are in God's hand though their deaths seem like destruction; this challenges the near-life assumption by locating life beyond visible survival.
The righteous may appear punished before people, but their hope is full of immortality; this gives the commentary's “more enduring” life a Jewish apocalyptic counterpart.
A tortured brother says the King of the universe will raise those who die for his laws to everlasting life; his choice under threat dramatizes preferring God's promise to present survival.

Another brother says it is better to die at human hands while hoping for resurrection than to be raised to life without it; the scene makes the commentary's unstated comparison with the hereafter explicit.
The midrash expands the sale in Genesis 25 by treating Esau's act as contempt for the birthright; it sharpens why the meal is a misvaluation, not simply an exchange of food.
The Mishnah calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation there; its spatial image clarifies the commentary's “near” as a relation to what follows.

The Mishnah says one hour of repentance and good deeds here is better than the whole life of the world to come, yet one hour's bliss there is better than all this world's life; this preserves the commentary's hierarchy while showing why present deeds still matter.
Jesus says the heart follows the treasure one stores; this makes the commentary's account of “preference” as a practiced direction of love more precise than a single cold calculation.
Jesus says no one can serve both God and Mammon; the divided allegiance directly frames the commentary's question of which claimant receives first place.
Jesus tells hearers to seek God's kingdom first, with food and clothing discussed around it; the verse turns the commentary's critique of daily ordering into a positive order of priorities.

column5: sell all for the hidden treasure
column6: The finder joyfully sells everything to obtain the field with its treasure; this reverses 87:16's direction by treating the coming kingdom as worth preferring to present holdings.
Jesus says the one who loses life for his sake will find it; this counters the commentary's assumption that keeping present life is the sure measure of life.
Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world and forfeiting one's life; the explicit trade-off supplies the comparison left unstated in the commentary's ayah 87:16.
The rich man leaves grieving because he has many possessions after Jesus tells him to sell and follow; this is a narrative instance of preferring present wealth to the offered lasting life.

Jesus explains that life's anxieties, riches and pleasures choke the heard word so it bears no mature fruit; this links the commentary's avoidance of reminder to worldly attachments that take its place.
Jesus warns that life does not consist in the abundance of possessions; this directly separates the commentary's “near life” from the accumulation people may mistake for life itself.
The rich fool plans to store his goods and tell his soul to relax, eat, drink and be merry; this gives the commentary's daily preference for the near life a concrete voice.
God tells the rich fool that his life is demanded that night; the scene answers his present-focused plan with the limit of the life he tried to secure.
Jesus concludes that this is the fate of one who stores for himself but is not rich toward God; the contrast specifies what the commentary's wrong ordering costs.

Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things during his life while Lazarus received bad, but now their situations are reversed; the parable makes the commentary's present/future comparison a scene of changed fortunes.
Jesus tells the crowd to work for food that endures to eternal life, not perishable food; this answers the commentary's image of near life as the readily consumed pasture.

column5: life in this world and eternal life
column6: Jesus says that the one who loves life in this world loses it, while the one who hates it keeps it for eternal life; this is the closest direct formulation of the commentary's ranking, with the important qualification that it is Jesus' saying.

column5: mind set on flesh or Spirit
column6: Paul says the mindset of the flesh is death while the Spirit's mindset is life and peace; the verse joins inner orientation to the outcome, like the commentary's preference and its consequence.
Paul says those using the world should not be absorbed by it because its present form is passing; this gives a concrete reason not to enthrone what the commentary calls near.
Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal; the distinction states why the commentary's near life is not the final measure.

Paul tells each person to look to the interests of others, not only their own; this gives a direct ethical counterpoint to the source commentary's explanation of īthār as preferring another over oneself.

Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God's people rather than the fleeting pleasure of sin; as the same Moses named in the commentary's final pages, he embodies preference for a lasting good over immediate pleasure.

Hebrews says Moses considered reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looked to the reward; the same figure named by the commentary models the opposite ordering of near wealth and future good.

The patriarchs, including Abraham, desire a better heavenly country rather than return to the one they left; this connects the commentary's mention of Abraham's pages with a concrete orientation beyond the near homeland.
Hebrews recalls Esau selling his birthright for one meal; its reuse of Genesis makes the commentary's preference-for-the-near pattern an explicit warning against trading away a lasting inheritance.
Hebrews says believers have no lasting city here but seek the one to come; this spells out the temporal contrast carried by the commentary's “near” life.
John warns against loving the world and its desires; the commentary likewise locates the failure in where love and priority are given, not in lack of information.
John says the world and its desire pass away, while the one doing God's will abides forever; this closely joins the commentary's near life, continuing action and lasting alternative.
Paul says Demas deserted him because he loved the present age; this concrete abandonment of costly work for current life gives the commentary's diagnosis a personal example.
Paul tells the rich to store a good foundation for the future so they may take hold of real life; this redirects possessions toward what the commentary calls more enduring.
Peter applies Isaiah's grass-and-flower image to mortal life; this brings the commentary's pasture and withering motif into the Christian proclamation of the enduring word.

Peter says the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it with the gospel preached to the readers; this connects the commentary's passing life with the old, transmitted message of its final verses.
Paul says what was written beforehand was written for instruction and hope; this supplies a Christian account of how the commentary's ancient pages can still address current hearers.
Timothy has known sacred writings from childhood, which can make him wise for salvation; this makes the commentary's inherited pages an active guide rather than merely an old report.
Paul says the wilderness events happened as examples and were written for later generations; this turns ancestral tracks into a record that later hearers can either heed or repeat.
Paul contrasts sowing to the flesh, which reaps corruption, with sowing to the Spirit, which reaps eternal life; this links repeated present conduct to what follows it.
The dead are judged from books according to their deeds; this gives the commentary's secondary image of traces left by one's steps a concrete judgment scene.
The proverb pictures wealth sprouting wings and flying away; it offers a specific image for the commentary's warning that what is given first place in near life cannot be kept.

Israel abandons the fountain of living water for cracked cisterns that hold none; unlike the commentary's focus on misranking rather than ignorance, this sharper indictment shows the biblical contrast between a lasting source and chosen substitutes.

column5: high and lofty, with the lowly
column6: The One who is high and inhabits eternity also dwells with the contrite and lowly; this adds a biblical counterpoint to the commentary's vertical contrast between the Most High and the “low” near life.
Qoheleth says God brings every deed, including the hidden, into judgment; this concretizes the commentary's image of choices leaving a trace that later identifies the walker.

Ben Sira urges the reader not to deprive himself of a happy day; read with his surrounding reminders of death, this is a Jewish countervoice that treats present goods as gifts to use rather than a life to enthrone.
Ben Sira compares human life to a garment that wears out; the image adds mortality to his counsel to enjoy a present day without mistaking it for permanence.

Ezra's angel says the Most High made not one world but two; this gives the commentary's near/after contrast an apocalyptic Jewish frame, though the verse itself does not rank every present good as evil.

Paul says people knew God yet failed to honor or thank him; unlike the commentary's explicit restraint from accusing its hearers of ignorance or denial, Paul makes culpable knowledge part of his diagnosis.

Paul describes an exchange of the Creator's truth for a lie and worship of the creature; this gives a sharper idolatry account of misdirected allegiance than the commentary's narrower charge of preferring near life.
Paul urges humility that counts others more significant than oneself; this carries the self-giving side of the source commentary's Arabic-root discussion into a Christian ethical instruction.
James compares human life to a mist that appears briefly and vanishes; this gives the commentary's “near life” a concrete limit while its next verse makes plans conditional on the Lord's will.

The risen Jesus names the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms as written witnesses; this is a Christian interpretive claim about older scriptures that adds context to the commentary's appeal to Abraham's and Moses' pages.

Augustine explains the earthly and heavenly cities through opposed loves, self-love and love of God; this reads the commentary's repeated “preference” as the allegiance that forms a person's community, not merely a choice of possessions.

Paul says he bears the marks of Jesus on his body; beside the source commentary's secondary link from preference to bodily trace and its reference to the mark of prostration, this makes allegiance visible in a person's scars, though the marks have different causes.

The Lamb's followers bear his and his Father's name on their foreheads; this is a concrete Christian mark of allegiance that can be set beside the commentary's face-mark from prostration, while keeping their distinct settings clear.
Israel is commanded to repeat the words to children in ordinary daily settings; this gives a concrete Hebrew Bible practice for the commentary's image of a saying transmitted across generations.

Paul says everyone appears before Christ's judgment seat to receive for what was done through the body; the bodily actions that the commentary figures as unseen traces thus have an explicit accounting counterpart.
After the first humans disobey, they are told they will return to dust; this gives the commentary's “near life” a concrete mortal boundary that makes the later-life comparison meaningful.

God bars the humans from taking the tree of life and living forever; the narrative distinguishes present human life from life without end, sharpening the commentary's contrast between near and enduring life.

Moses says the commandments are to be bound as a sign on the hand and frontlets between the eyes; this joins transmitted divine words to a visible bodily marker, beside the commentary's secondary mark-and-remembrance imagery.

Moses tells Israel to remember former days and ask fathers and elders to recount them; this supplies a concrete practice of transmitted memory beside the commentary's image of a saying handed down from Abraham and Moses.

Ezekiel says God takes no pleasure in anyone's death and calls Israel to turn and live; this adds repentance as a still-open alternative to the commentary's repeated, changeable preference for the near life.

column5: feasting without regard for God's work
column6: Isaiah depicts music and wine while people do not regard YHWH's work; this is a specific scene of present enjoyment displacing attention to divine action, close to the commentary's claim that worldly attachments crowd out reminder.

The person who trusts YHWH is like a tree by water whose leaves stay green and which does not cease bearing fruit; this reverses the commentary's withering pasture image by showing what enduring life rooted in God looks like.

Those who fear YHWH speak together, and a book of remembrance is written before him; this makes the commentary's secondary image of choices leaving a trace a specific written record tied to reverence.

Jeremiah says the nations inherited lies from their fathers; beside the commentary's account of people following ancestral footprints, this is a counterexample where the inherited trail must be rejected.

The man in linen marks the foreheads of those grieving Jerusalem's abominations so they are distinguished in the coming judgment; this gives the commentary's mark-on-body motif a concrete biblical scene, though its mark signifies grief rather than prayer.

Jesus tells a host to invite the poor, disabled and blind rather than guests who can return the favor; this concretizes the self-preference reversal that the source commentary explains through īthār and its positive use for giving others priority.

Jesus says the host who gives without repayment will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous; this joins the commentary's self-giving preference to the future life that outweighs present return.

The Jerusalem believers sell property so no one among them is needy; this is a concrete communal counterpart to the commentary's account of the Helpers preferring the newcomers over themselves despite scarcity.

Paul's Greek says believers should take the lead in honoring one another; beside the source commentary's gloss of īthār as putting something first and its positive case of preferring others, this is a close ethical parallel without a claim of shared roots.

Paul says one community's present abundance should supply another's need, with the possibility of reciprocal help later; this gives a practical form to the commentary's positive choice to give the other person priority.
In response to disciples seeking rank, Jesus says the great one among them must be their servant; this reverses the commentary's image of giving the preferred object the head place.
Jesus says the Son of Man came to serve and give his life as a ransom for many; this extends the commentary's positive “prefer another” ethic to the giving of one's own life.

Paul describes opponents whose god is their belly and whose minds are set on earthly things; this concretely identifies appetites and earthly orientation as a rival allegiance to the one valued in the commentary.
Paul contrasts that earthly orientation with believers' citizenship in heaven; this gives the commentary's near-life/afterlife distinction a communal identity and destination.
Paul commands hearers to set their minds on things above rather than things on earth; this directly addresses the commentary's claim that the issue is the repeated direction of preference.
Paul says that when Christ, the believers' life, appears, they too will appear with him in glory; this names a future life hidden from present view, beyond the commentary's near life.
The addressees accept the plundering of their property because they know they have a better and abiding possession; this is a direct case of relinquishing near goods for what lasts.

Paul compares disciplined faithfulness to runners in a race who run to obtain a prize; this gives a concrete race image for the commentary's surah-wide sequence in which simply being first does not settle the outcome.
Paul contrasts a perishable athletic crown with the imperishable one sought by believers; this adds an explicit durable prize to the commentary's image of the later good as more lasting.

Jesus cites the place where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched; this is a distinct punishment formula beside the commentary's reference to the one who neither dies nor lives in the great fire.

Jesus ends the judgment scene with eternal punishment for some and eternal life for the righteous; this makes the two enduring outcomes explicit beside the commentary's ranking of near life and the hereafter.

Jesus tells Martha that he is the resurrection and the life, and that the believer will live even after dying; this answers the commentary's contrast between merely present life and life beyond death.

column5: death ends in the new creation
column6: The new Jerusalem vision says death, mourning, crying and pain will be no more; it gives a concrete positive horizon to the commentary's contrast with a life that does not truly live.

Wisdom says the one who finds her finds life and receives favor from YHWH; this presents life as the result of choosing a path of instruction, matching the commentary's choice-versus-ignorance distinction.
Wisdom says the one who misses her harms himself and loves death; this makes a person's preference itself the source of the outcome, as the commentary says the hearers know the way but rank wrongly.

column5: the command is not far away
column6: Moses says the command is not too difficult or far away; with verse 14's word near in mouth and heart, this offers a spatial counter-image to the commentary's explanation that “near life” is named by its distance from what follows.
Qoheleth says a person leaves life as naked as at birth and cannot carry away labor's gain; this specifies why the commentary's near possessions cannot be the more enduring good.

Isaiah's final vision shows the corpses of rebels with worm and fire that do not cease; this supplies a Hebrew Bible punishment image related to, but distinct from, the commentary's “neither die nor live” formula.

The passage describes the world to come without eating, drinking or commerce, with the righteous enjoying the radiance of the Divine Presence; it gives rabbinic content to the commentary's enduring alternative while distinguishing it from present bodily life.
The treatise argues that reason can govern the passions; this gives a Jewish philosophical account of the self-ordering behind the commentary's repeated choice of what receives precedence.

Jesus tells his hearers not to be anxious about life and what they will eat or drink, since life is more than food; this qualifies the commentary's criticism by treating present needs as real but not life's highest measure.

Jesus says Mary chose the good portion while Martha is distracted by service; this makes preference for hearing the teacher's word a domestic scene, adding a specific example to the commentary's contrast between reminder and competing attention.

column5: not shaped by the present age
column6: Paul tells the community not to be conformed to this age but to be transformed in mind; this connects present-age pressure to an ongoing reordering of judgment.

Peter says believers were redeemed from the futile ways handed down by their ancestors; this is a Christian counterexample to the ancestral footprints in the commentary, showing inheritance can also be abandoned.

Hebrews tells its hearers to lay aside every weight and run the race set before them with endurance; the shared race image adds disciplined persistence to the commentary's surah-wide sequence, though the passage focuses on faithfulness rather than worldly preference.

The saying calls the world a corpse and says it is unworthy of the one who has understood it; this is a deliberately harsher counter-reading than the source commentary, which locates the fault in preferring near life rather than declaring that life itself is dead.

Augustine says the heavenly city's pilgrims use the earthly city's peace during their journey while desiring the peace above; this interprets present life as a provisional good, qualifying any reading of the commentary as requiring escape from all earthly life.
